notes.text: Sarah saw the son of the Egyptian mocking — Mocking Isaac no doubt, for it is sad, with reference to this, Gal. iv, 29, that he that was born after the flesh, persecuted him that was born after the spirit. Ishmael is here called the son of the Egyptian, because (as some think) the four hundred years affliction of the seed of Abraham by the Egyptians began now, and was to be dated from hence.

Cast out the bond-woman — This was a type of the rejection of the unbelieving Jews, who, though they were the seed of Abraham, yet, because they submitted not to the gospel-covenant, were unchurched and disfranchised. And that, which above any thing provoked God to cast them off, was, their mocking and persecuting the gospel-church, God's Isaac, in his infancy.
The thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight — it grieved him that Ishmael had given such provocation. And still more that Sarah insisted upon such a punishment.

The casting out of Ishmael was not his ruin. He shall be a nation because he is thy seed — We are not sure that it was his eternal ruin. It is presumption to say, that all these who are left out of the external dispensation of God's covenant are excluded from all his mercies. Those may be saved who are not thus honoured.
And Abraham rose up early in the morning — We may suppose immediately after he had in the night-visions received orders to do this.

God heard the voice of the lad — We read not of a word be said; but his sighs and groans, cried loud in the ears of the God of mercy. An angel was sent to comfort Hagar, who assures her, God has heard the voice of the lad where he is - Though he be in the wilderness; for wherever we are, there is a way open heavenwards; therefore lift up the lad, and hold him in thy hand - God's readiness to help us when we are in trouble must not slacken, but quicken our endeavours to help ourselves. He repeats the promise concerning her son, that he should be a great nation, as a reason why she should bestir herself to help him.

glossa.text:
« The child grew therefore, » etc. He grows who, disposing ascents in his heart, comes to the solid food of doctrine. Whence, grow, and thou shalt eat me.

« He grew, » etc. ((AUG.)) Not on the day of his son's birth, nor on the day of his circumcision, but on the day of his weaning did he make a feast: because great ought to be the joy of the spiritual age, when a man has been made such as may be fed with solid food, like to those to whom it is said I Cor. III: « I gave you milk to drink, not meat. »

« And when Sara had seen. » etc. ((HIER.)) This is expounded in two ways: either that he made sport for idols, according to that of Exod. XXXII: « The people sat down to eat and to drink, and they rose up to play. » Or that against Isaac, as standing in the place of the elder in age, he claimed the birthright for himself; which Sara hearing did not bear.

« Cast out this bondwoman, » etc. ((BED., c. 21; ISID., c. 17, in Gen.)) It is asked: why did Sara before wish to receive a son by the bondwoman, or why does she now bid him be cast out with his mother? Which she does not do inflamed with jealousy, but compelled by the mystery of prophecy. For Agar, according to the Apostle, brought forth the carnal people unto bondage; but Sara the spiritual and free people, with which freedom Christ has set us free. It was signified therefore by this mystery that the former people, begotten in bondage, does not remain in the house of Sara, that is, of the Church, for ever, nor is heir or partner of Christians, nor possesses the kingdom of glory together with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.

« He took it hard, » etc. ((AUG.)) It is asked why Abraham was made sorrowful, since this was a prophecy which he rather than Sara ought to have known: but Sara said from revelation what had first been revealed to her. He however was moved by a father's affection, to whom the Lord afterwards revealed it. Or perhaps both of them at first knew not what it was, and it was prophesied through Sara who knew it not, when she was moved with a woman's mind on account of the bondwoman's pride.

« For thy seed. » ((AUG.)) It is to be noted that Ismael also was called by God the seed of Abraham, whereas the Apostle says Rom. IX: « Not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise shall be counted in the seed. » But this belongs properly to Isaac, who is not the son of the flesh, but of the promise, and is spiritual seed from the promise, not from the flesh.

« Taking bread. » etc. ((ALC. EX BEDA, c. 21.)) When therefore Abraham cast out Agar, taking bread, he laid it upon her shoulders for this cause, etc. *as far as* because certain of the people are to seek refuge under the shadow of the wood of the cross.

« He took bread and a bottle of water. » ((AUG. Q. in Gen. tom. III.)) It is asked: how did he lay upon her shoulders a boy so great? For he who, before Isaac was born, had been circumcised at thirteen years old, when Abraham was ninety-nine, and Isaac was born when his father was a hundred; and Ismael was playing with Isaac when Sara was moved, doubtless with a boy somewhat grown, who had already been weaned: assuredly he was more than sixteen years old when he was driven out with his mother. But granting that we take what is said of his playing with the little one as said by recapitulation, before Isaac was weaned; even so a boy of more than thirteen years could not be laid upon his mother's shoulders; but it must be supplied, he gave over her boy, etc.

« He laid it on her shoulder. » ((HIER. in Q. Hebr.)) When Isaac was born, Ismael was thirteen years old, and after his weaning he is driven out with his mother. Among the Hebrews the opinion varies, some asserting the time of his weaning to have been appointed at the fifth year, others at the twelfth. We therefore, that we may choose the shorter age, reckon Ismael to have been cast out with his mother after eighteen years, and that it did not befit one already a youth to have sat upon his mother's neck. But that idiom of the Hebrew tongue is true, that every son is called an infant and a little one in comparison with his parents. At Rome too, even to this day, all sons are called infants.

« She cast the boy. » etc. ((HIER.)) That which follows: « And she cast the boy under one fir tree, and going away sat over against him afar off, as it were a bowshot. » For she said: I shall not see the death of my little one, and she sat over against him; and at once it is joined. And the boy cried out and wept; and the Lord heard the voice of the boy from heaven, where he was, and the angel said to Agar: Let nothing move. For in the Hebrew this is written first: « I shall not see the death of my boy. » So it is read consequently, that Agar sat over against the boy, and lifted up her voice, and wept, and God heard the voice of the little one. For while the mother wept and awaited the death of her son, God heard the boy, whom he had promised should be for a great nation. For the mother bewails not her own death, but her son's.

((AUG. Q. in Gen., tom. III.)) It is asked how the mother, etc., *as far as* as those walking, of whatever age, often do.

« And he heard. » ((BED. et ISID. ubi supra.)) The boy cries out weeping, and God heard him; and, an angel showing it, she beholds the fountain, and it is said for those who are converted to Christ, and who, weeping for their sins, are heard, and with the eyes of the heart opened see the fountain of water, that is, Christ, who says Joan. VII « He that thirsteth, let him come to me and drink. » The angel signifies Elias, through whom the people is to believe. Whence Malach. IV: « Behold I will send you Elias, who shall turn the hearts of the fathers unto the children. » 

« The angel of the Lord. » ((ISID.)) In that Scripture pronounces him who speaks to Agar first an angel, afterwards the Lord, he is to be believed to have been the Son of God, who spoke through the law and the prophets, who through obedience to the Father's will is called an angel, but according to nature is God.

notes.text: Holy — Sincerely devoted to thy service.

glossa.text: *For I am holy.* ((AUG.)) Christ properly holy, sanctifying, etc., *as far as* have mercy on him that cries, gladden him that is lifted up.
*Meek.* ((ID.)) Bearing man, until he perfect him, etc., *as far as* when he is not yet perfect.
*Give ear.* ((CASS.)) See the order of the prayer, etc., *as far as* a hearing to my supplication.
*Of tribulation.* ((AUG., CASS.)) When one cries more earnestly, etc., *as far as because there is none like to thee among the gods, O Lord.*

*All whom thou hast made shall come and adore before,* etc. ((AUG.)) If there is a nation which God did not make, that one shall not adore. He announces the Church spread abroad everywhere, which is now fulfilled: And note that, as the Scripture says: *In a broad nation is the glory of the king, in the diminishing of the people is the ruin of the prince.* There follows: *And they shall glorify the name.*
*Thou art God alone.* ((ID.)) Or thou alone art great against those to come, who call themselves great and gods.

notes.text: The apostle here sets himself more fully to vindicate his doctrine from the consequence above suggested, chap. iii, 7, 8. He had then only in strong terms denied and renounced it: here he removes the very foundation thereof.
Dead to sin — Freed both from the guilt and from the power of it.

As many as have been baptized into Jesus Christ have been baptized into his death — In baptism we, through faith, are ingrafted into Christ; and we draw new spiritual life from this new root, through his Spirit, who fashions us like unto him, and particularly with regard to his death and resurrection.

We are buried with him — Alluding to the ancient manner of baptizing by immersion. That as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory - Glorious power. Of the Father, so we also, by the same power, should rise again; and as he lives a new life in heaven, so we should walk in newness of life. This, says the apostle, our very baptism represents to us.
For — Surely these two must go together; so that if we are indeed made conformable to his death, we shall also know the power of his resurrection.

Our old man — Coeval with our being, and as old as the fall; our evil nature; a strong and beautiful expression for that entire depravity and corruption which by nature spreads itself over the whole man, leaving no part uninfected. This in a believer is crucified with Christ, mortified, gradually killed, by virtue of our union with him. That the body of sin - All evil tempers, words, and actions, which are the "members" of the "old man," Colossians iii, 5, might be destroyed.
For he that is dead — With Christ. Is freed from the guilt of past, and from the power of present, sin, as dead men from the commands of their former masters.
Dead with Christ — Conformed to his death, by dying to sin.
He died to sin — To atone for and abolish it. He liveth unto God - A glorious eternal life, such as we shall live also.

glossa.text: *Shall we continue.* This perverse men take from that word: *Where the offence abounded, grace also did more abound.* To say this is to be ungrateful to grace. And because grace is strong where the offence abounded, one must not continue in sin, as some reckon, for the sake of greater grace. For grace did more abound where the offence abounded, not by the merit of him who sins, but by the help of him who succours. One must not therefore continue in sin, but rather we ought and are able to be, as it were, dead to sin and buried through that same grace, and to rise again unto justice, and afterwards unto eternal life.

*We are dead.* That is, freed from sin through baptism, so that it may no longer have dominion in us, through grace. For to die to sin is to be freed from sin. *How shall we yet,* etc. For since grace has granted this, that we should die to sin, what else do we do if we live in it, but that we should be ungrateful to grace?

*Know you not.* Being dead to sin, which is done in baptism, we ought not to live to it again, so that it should be necessary to die to it again: because in the death of Christ, that is, in the likeness of the death of Christ, that as he died once in the flesh and lives always, so we, having died once to evil through baptism, may always live to good. Or he says *in the death:* because death is the cause of this purification.

*Buried together.* Whatever was done in the cross of Christ, in the burial, in the resurrection, in the ascension, in the sitting at the right hand, was so done that the Christian life might be conformed to these things, which were mystically not only spoken but also done. Consider the several things of Christ, in whom the old man had lived according to punishment, hunger, thirst and the like, not according to fault: in this manner he ended and disposed the oldness, so that, enduring the pain of the cross, he had his limbs thus stretched out and fastened, that they might not be moved to their former acts, from which, buried also, he rested, withdrawn from human sight, requiring of us that we lay aside the oldness of sins with the sorrow and groaning of penance: that our limbs be fastened together through continence and justice, lest we return to our former evils, from which we should so perfectly rest that neither the sight nor the memory of them be had: and not only does he require this of us in the sacrament of the passion, but he also brings it about, if we will to imitate him. *He rose again from the dead.* The death and the resurrection of Christ are also sacraments.

*The old man.* That is, the old acts are crucified, that is, dead. Our oldness and our curse consist in two things, namely in fault and in punishment. But Christ by his single oldness consumed our twofold one. For in the sepulchre he rested one day and two nights. By the one day his single oldness is signified, but by the two nights our twofold one; whence: Christ blotted out our fault, present, past, and future. The past by forgiving it, the present by drawing us back from it, the future by conferring grace that we might avoid it. The punishment likewise he consumed, wholly blotting out the punishment of Gehenna, so that they who truly repent may not feel it. The temporal punishment, however, he did not entirely take away: for hunger, thirst, death and the like remain; but he cast down its reign and dominion, and at the last he will utterly destroy it.

*Knowing that Christ. (AUG)*. One rose again now not to die. Lazarus rose again, but to die; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose again, but to die; the son of the widow rose again, but to die: Christ rose again not to die. Hear the Apostle, *Christ rising again,* etc. Hope for such a resurrection, and for the sake of this be a Christian, not for the sake of the happiness of this earth.

*For in that he died to sin. ((AUG.))* The Apostle commends the sacrament of baptism, that as he, by dying once, is preached as having died by a likeness of sin, so whoever has been baptized in him may die to that same thing of which that was the likeness, that is, to sin; and may live by being born again from the font, as he lived by rising again from the sepulchre.
*So do you also.* Whatever he said above belongs to men through the grace of Christ, here he attributes to the Romans.

notes.text: Luke vi, 30; John xv, 20.
How much more — This cannot refer to the quantity of reproach and persecution: (for in this the servant cannot be above his Lord:) but only to the certainty of it. Matt. xii, 24.

Therefore fear them not — For ye have only the same usage with your Lord. There is nothing covered - So that however they may slander you now, your innocence will at length appear. Mark iv, 22; Luke viii, 17; xii, 2.

Even what I now tell you secretly is not to be kept secret long, but declared publicly. Therefore, What ye hear in the ear, publish on the house-top — Two customs of the Jews seem to be alluded to here. Their doctors used to whisper in the ear of their disciples what they were to pronounce aloud to others. And as their houses were low and flat roofed, they sometimes preached to the people from thence. Luke xii, 3.

And be not afraid — of any thing which ye may suffer for proclaiming it. Be afraid of him who is able to destroy both body and soul in hell - It is remarkable, that our Lord commands those who love God, still to fear him, even on this account, under this notion.

The particular providence of God is another reason for your not fearing man. For this extends to the very smallest things. And if he has such care over the most inconsiderable creatures, how much more will he take care of you, (provided you confess him before men, before powerful enemies of the truth, ) and that not only in this life, but in the other also?

Whosoever shall confess me — Publicly acknowledge me for the promised Messiah. But this confession implies the receiving his whole doctrine, Mark viii, 38, and obeying all his commandments. Luke ix, 26.

Whosoever shall deny me before men — To which ye will be strongly tempted. For Think not that I am come - That is, think not that universal peace will be the immediate consequence of my coming. Just the contrary. Both public and private divisions will follow, wheresoever my Gospel comes with power. Ye - this is not the design, though it be the event of his coming, through the opposition of devils and men.
And the foes of a man — That loves and follows me. Micah vii, 6.
He that loveth father or mother more than me — He that is not ready to give up all these, when they stand in competition with his duty.
He that taketh not his cross — That is, whatever pain or inconvenience cannot be avoided, but by doing some evil, or omitting some good. Matt. xvi, 24; Luke xiv, 27.

He that findeth his life shall lose it — He that saves his life by denying me, shall lose it eternally; and he that loseth his life by confessing me, shall save it eternally. And as you shall be thus rewarded, so in proportion shall they who entertain you for my sake. Matt. xvi, 25; John xii, 25.

glossa.text: *The disciple is not,* etc. Do not disdain to bear what I bear, who am the Lord, doing what I will, and the master teaching what I know to be useful.

*If the master of the house.* He shows his own calumnies, that by his example they may bear injuries. Whence he said: *Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. Beelzebub.* Beel is Bel himself, Zebub, a fly, etc., *as far as* the man of flies, or having flies.

*Therefore fear them not.* Their savagery or their blasphemies, because the day will come when God shall judge the hidden things of men, where both their wickedness shall be uncovered, and your intention, now known to God alone, shall be known by all.
*What I tell you.* That is, in what I wish you to be constant, etc., *as far as* the dwelling-place of the flesh being trodden underfoot, *preach ye.*

*Upon.* He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, etc., *as far as* tell it in the whole world. *Are not two sparrows?* Luke: *Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings ((Luc. XII))*? Nor is there much difference, seeing that two go for an as, and five for a dipondius. For a dipondius is out of two asses. And what one is in numbers, that the as is in weight: and what two is, that is the dipondius. *And one of them.* How then does the Apostle say: *Doth God take care for oxen ((Luc. IX))*? But care is one thing, knowledge another.
*Numbered.* That is, by the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* small and idle words should lie hidden from him.
*Whosoever shall confess.* Or a man confesses Jesus with that faith which works by love: he denies who does not obey the precepts of God.

*But he that.* He is denied by the Son before the Father, to whom there is not manifested, in the power of the divinity, the Son and the Father. He is confessed by the Son before the Father, who through the Son has access to the Father.
*Peace.* A good war was sent, that an evil peace might be broken.

*For I came.* Here Luke says: *There shall be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three shall be divided.* How then, etc., *as far as* circumcision and the other carnal observances. *To set apart.* That is, to extinguish the private affections of the flesh, by which men so love one another that they serve God the less. Or that they be utterly turned away, not that father and mother are not to be honoured, but after God; this is the order of charity.
*He that loveth father.* After God they are to be loved, but if both cannot be kept, hatred toward one's own is piety toward God.

*And he that taketh not,* etc. The cross is borne in two ways, etc., *as far as* the love of Christ may be shown. *And followeth me.* For one man mortifies the flesh for empty glory, or has a carnal compassion for his neighbour so as to favour his fault: he seems to bear the cross, but does not follow the Lord.
*He that findeth,* etc. By the name of the soul the present life is designated.

I was there to hear your borning cry
At the font we start our journey

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A type of death-and-resurrection-to-life that early Christian reading connected to Christ's raising; resonates with 6:4-5,8-9 union in death and resurrection. Faint and contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover of this sickness.” But Yahweh’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel, that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
echoes.note: 'Beelzebul' (10:25) derives from Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consults. The name of the rejected foreign deity becomes the slander hurled at 'the master of the house'; the disciples should expect the same naming, 'how much more those of his household.'

echoes.text: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.
echoes.note: 'Neither fear ye their fear... Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.' Isaiah's command to fear God rather than the conspiracy of men is the precise logic of 10:28: do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who can destroy soul and body. The double 'do not fear / rather fear' structure is Isaianic.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind. Therefore behold, the days come”, says Yahweh, “that it shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter; for they shall bury in Topheth, until there is no place to bury.
echoes.note: 'Gehenna' (10:28) is the valley of Hinnom (Topheth), the site of child-sacrifice that Jeremiah declares will become 'the valley of slaughter.' The OT condemnation of this valley as the place of fiery judgment supplies the term for the place where God can destroy both soul and body.

echoes.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
echoes.note: Josiah defiles Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so none could pass a child through fire to Molech. Reinforces the Gehenna background as the defiled valley of fire that becomes the figure of final destruction (10:28).

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: 'There shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground.' The idiom of every hair guarded as a token of total providential protection (cf. 2 Sam 14:11; 1 Kgs 1:52) lies directly behind 10:30, 'the very hairs of your head are all numbered,' assuring the disciples of God's exhaustive care amid persecution.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: God keeps count of the sufferer's wanderings and bottles his tears. A thematic analogue to the divine bookkeeping of hairs and the fall of sparrows (10:29-31) — God's minute attention to the afflicted — though without verbal overlap.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' The wisdom maxim that proper fear is owed to God alone undergirds the redirection of fear in 10:28, but the connection is general rather than verbal.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.' A faint analogue to confessing Christ before men without shame (10:32), continuous with the 'testimony before governors and kings' of 10:18. Disputed and thematic only.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 10:35-36 is a near-verbatim rendering of Micah 7:6: 'the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Matthew reproduces the three paired antagonisms (father/son here as father, daughter/mother, daughter-in-law/mother-in-law) and the climactic 'a man's foes will be those of his own household' almost word for word. This is the strongest, formula-grade allusion in the chapter.

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi 'said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren... for they have observed thy word.' The blessing praises placing covenant loyalty above family bonds — the same demand as 10:37, loving God above father, mother, son, daughter. A recognized OT precedent for cult loyalty overriding kinship.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites slay brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command and are thereby 'consecrated.' A harsh background for loyalty to God dividing even kin (10:34-37); thematically apt but lexically distant and contested.

echoes.text: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]
echoes.note: The Aqedah — Abraham not withholding his son for the sake of God — is a possible figural backdrop to 'he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me' (10:37): supreme love of God above the dearest child. Suggestive typology rather than verbal echo.

notes.text: Hast prevailed — Thou prevailedst against me. Jeremiah at first excused himself to God, chap. i, 6, but the Lord prevailed against him replying, ver. i, 7, Say not, I am a child, for thou shalt go to all that I shall send thee, and whatsoever I command thee thou shalt speak, ver. i, 9. This is all that is here meant, namely, God's over-ruling him contrary to his own inclinations.

Since — Since I first began to be a prophet, I have faithfully discharged my office, and that with warmth and zeal. Spoil - I have prophesied that violence and spoil was coming. Because - Because of that scorn and derision with which they treated him.
I said — He did not speak this openly, but in his heart. But - He found in his heart a constraint to go on.
Prevail — Desiring nothing more than that I might be enticed to speak or do something which they might make matter of a colourable accusation.

But — The prophet recovering himself out of his fit of passion, encourageth himself in his God, whom he calls the mighty and terrible one, so declaring his faith in the power of God, as one able to save him, and in the promise and good will of God toward him; therefore he saith, The Lord is with me; such was the promise of God to this prophet, when he first undertook the prophetical office, chap. i, 8. Be not afraid of their faces, for I am with thee to deliver thee saith the Lord: from hence be concludes, that though he had many that pursued after his life, yet they should stumble in their ways of violence, and should not prevail. Ashamed - That they should be ashamed of what they had done, or be brought to shame for what they had done; for prosper they should not: or they acted like fools, and did not deal prudently for themselves (so this word is translated, Isaiah lii, 13,) yea, they should become a reproach, and their reproach should be a lasting perpetual reproach that should not be forgotten.

glossa.text:
*Thou hast deceived me, O Lord. ((ID.))* The prophet says that he was deceived by the Lord, etc., *as far as* he may endure persecutions and straits.

*I am become a derision. ((ID.))* The prophet had thought that what the Lord threatened would come at once; and the people reckoned that what had not come at once was not going to come.

*And thou, O Lord of hosts,* etc. ((ID.)) God alone is, etc., *as far as* therefore dead in his sins.

*Let me see.* Although the just man knows that he has God for his defender, yet in the patience of human frailty he desires to see even now what he knows is to come.

*For to thee.* Thou who sayest: *Vengeance to me, and I will repay* ((Heb. X)), etc. Happy the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord: whence the Apostle: *All that is made manifest is light ((Ephes. V))*.

*Because he hath delivered. ((ID.))* The poor in spirit, having obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises him, and glories that he has been snatched from the hand of the worst of men. But this comes about not by merit, but by the grace of him who set the poor man free, who loves not the riches of a pride that is falling, but the humility of the poor man set free.

notes.text: For thy sake — For my obedience to thy commands, and zeal for thy glory.

Zeal — That fervent love which I have for thy house and service, and glory, and people. Eaten - Exhausted my spirits. Upon me - I have been as deeply affected with thy reproaches, as with mine own. This tho' truly belonging to David, yet was also directed by the spirit of God in him, to represent the disposition and condition of Christ, in whom it was more fully accomplished, to whom therefore it is applied in the New Testament, the first part of it, John ii, 17, and the latter, Rom. xv, 3.
Wept — For their impiety. Reproach - They derided me for it.

glossa.text:
*Because for thy sake I have borne reproaches.* ((CAS.)) He gathers into one the many things he endured, to stir up odium against the Jews; *reproach:* he casts out demons in Beelzebub, a wine-bibber, a glutton. ((Matth. XI.))

*It hath covered.* This is wont to befall those torn in a good cause, who are wont to be made so much the sadder for a time as they know that wicked things are being fabricated against them.
*A stranger.* Or a guest, who is received into a house for a time; not as a most dear brother, which I was.

*The zeal of thy house hath eaten me up.* When with a cord he cast out them that sold. What follows upon this zeal he subjoins: *And the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me.* Because the Jews, being rebuked, cast their insults upon him like darts, as: *Is not this the son of Joseph? ((Luc. IV.)) Of them that reproach thee.* When they said: *Can God furnish a table in the wilderness? ((Psal. LXXVII.)) These are thy gods, O Israel ((Exod. XXXII))*. Whence he now says that the same insults fall upon himself which they formerly cast as reproaches, that thou mayest see that they did this out of impious custom and not newly.

*They are fallen.* ((CAS.)). Evils fall upon us when we cannot avoid them: *they are fallen,* therefore, that is, they took effect.

*And I covered it in fasting,* etc. ((AUG.)) I chose rather to fast than to take gall and vinegar; that is, the old and the bitter, who do not enter into his body. ((CAS.)) *And I covered.* I did not exercise power by avenging. *And it became,* which appeared in the spittings, *a reproach.* ((AUG.)) Of detractors and mockers.

notes.text: The apostle here sets himself more fully to vindicate his doctrine from the consequence above suggested, chap. iii, 7, 8. He had then only in strong terms denied and renounced it: here he removes the very foundation thereof.
Dead to sin — Freed both from the guilt and from the power of it.

As many as have been baptized into Jesus Christ have been baptized into his death — In baptism we, through faith, are ingrafted into Christ; and we draw new spiritual life from this new root, through his Spirit, who fashions us like unto him, and particularly with regard to his death and resurrection.

We are buried with him — Alluding to the ancient manner of baptizing by immersion. That as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory - Glorious power. Of the Father, so we also, by the same power, should rise again; and as he lives a new life in heaven, so we should walk in newness of life. This, says the apostle, our very baptism represents to us.
For — Surely these two must go together; so that if we are indeed made conformable to his death, we shall also know the power of his resurrection.

Our old man — Coeval with our being, and as old as the fall; our evil nature; a strong and beautiful expression for that entire depravity and corruption which by nature spreads itself over the whole man, leaving no part uninfected. This in a believer is crucified with Christ, mortified, gradually killed, by virtue of our union with him. That the body of sin - All evil tempers, words, and actions, which are the "members" of the "old man," Colossians iii, 5, might be destroyed.
For he that is dead — With Christ. Is freed from the guilt of past, and from the power of present, sin, as dead men from the commands of their former masters.
Dead with Christ — Conformed to his death, by dying to sin.
He died to sin — To atone for and abolish it. He liveth unto God - A glorious eternal life, such as we shall live also.

glossa.text: *Shall we continue.* This perverse men take from that word: *Where the offence abounded, grace also did more abound.* To say this is to be ungrateful to grace. And because grace is strong where the offence abounded, one must not continue in sin, as some reckon, for the sake of greater grace. For grace did more abound where the offence abounded, not by the merit of him who sins, but by the help of him who succours. One must not therefore continue in sin, but rather we ought and are able to be, as it were, dead to sin and buried through that same grace, and to rise again unto justice, and afterwards unto eternal life.

*We are dead.* That is, freed from sin through baptism, so that it may no longer have dominion in us, through grace. For to die to sin is to be freed from sin. *How shall we yet,* etc. For since grace has granted this, that we should die to sin, what else do we do if we live in it, but that we should be ungrateful to grace?

*Know you not.* Being dead to sin, which is done in baptism, we ought not to live to it again, so that it should be necessary to die to it again: because in the death of Christ, that is, in the likeness of the death of Christ, that as he died once in the flesh and lives always, so we, having died once to evil through baptism, may always live to good. Or he says *in the death:* because death is the cause of this purification.

*Buried together.* Whatever was done in the cross of Christ, in the burial, in the resurrection, in the ascension, in the sitting at the right hand, was so done that the Christian life might be conformed to these things, which were mystically not only spoken but also done. Consider the several things of Christ, in whom the old man had lived according to punishment, hunger, thirst and the like, not according to fault: in this manner he ended and disposed the oldness, so that, enduring the pain of the cross, he had his limbs thus stretched out and fastened, that they might not be moved to their former acts, from which, buried also, he rested, withdrawn from human sight, requiring of us that we lay aside the oldness of sins with the sorrow and groaning of penance: that our limbs be fastened together through continence and justice, lest we return to our former evils, from which we should so perfectly rest that neither the sight nor the memory of them be had: and not only does he require this of us in the sacrament of the passion, but he also brings it about, if we will to imitate him. *He rose again from the dead.* The death and the resurrection of Christ are also sacraments.

*The old man.* That is, the old acts are crucified, that is, dead. Our oldness and our curse consist in two things, namely in fault and in punishment. But Christ by his single oldness consumed our twofold one. For in the sepulchre he rested one day and two nights. By the one day his single oldness is signified, but by the two nights our twofold one; whence: Christ blotted out our fault, present, past, and future. The past by forgiving it, the present by drawing us back from it, the future by conferring grace that we might avoid it. The punishment likewise he consumed, wholly blotting out the punishment of Gehenna, so that they who truly repent may not feel it. The temporal punishment, however, he did not entirely take away: for hunger, thirst, death and the like remain; but he cast down its reign and dominion, and at the last he will utterly destroy it.

*Knowing that Christ. (AUG)*. One rose again now not to die. Lazarus rose again, but to die; the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue rose again, but to die; the son of the widow rose again, but to die: Christ rose again not to die. Hear the Apostle, *Christ rising again,* etc. Hope for such a resurrection, and for the sake of this be a Christian, not for the sake of the happiness of this earth.

*For in that he died to sin. ((AUG.))* The Apostle commends the sacrament of baptism, that as he, by dying once, is preached as having died by a likeness of sin, so whoever has been baptized in him may die to that same thing of which that was the likeness, that is, to sin; and may live by being born again from the font, as he lived by rising again from the sepulchre.
*So do you also.* Whatever he said above belongs to men through the grace of Christ, here he attributes to the Romans.

notes.text: Luke vi, 30; John xv, 20.
How much more — This cannot refer to the quantity of reproach and persecution: (for in this the servant cannot be above his Lord:) but only to the certainty of it. Matt. xii, 24.

Therefore fear them not — For ye have only the same usage with your Lord. There is nothing covered - So that however they may slander you now, your innocence will at length appear. Mark iv, 22; Luke viii, 17; xii, 2.

Even what I now tell you secretly is not to be kept secret long, but declared publicly. Therefore, What ye hear in the ear, publish on the house-top — Two customs of the Jews seem to be alluded to here. Their doctors used to whisper in the ear of their disciples what they were to pronounce aloud to others. And as their houses were low and flat roofed, they sometimes preached to the people from thence. Luke xii, 3.

And be not afraid — of any thing which ye may suffer for proclaiming it. Be afraid of him who is able to destroy both body and soul in hell - It is remarkable, that our Lord commands those who love God, still to fear him, even on this account, under this notion.

The particular providence of God is another reason for your not fearing man. For this extends to the very smallest things. And if he has such care over the most inconsiderable creatures, how much more will he take care of you, (provided you confess him before men, before powerful enemies of the truth, ) and that not only in this life, but in the other also?

Whosoever shall confess me — Publicly acknowledge me for the promised Messiah. But this confession implies the receiving his whole doctrine, Mark viii, 38, and obeying all his commandments. Luke ix, 26.

Whosoever shall deny me before men — To which ye will be strongly tempted. For Think not that I am come - That is, think not that universal peace will be the immediate consequence of my coming. Just the contrary. Both public and private divisions will follow, wheresoever my Gospel comes with power. Ye - this is not the design, though it be the event of his coming, through the opposition of devils and men.
And the foes of a man — That loves and follows me. Micah vii, 6.
He that loveth father or mother more than me — He that is not ready to give up all these, when they stand in competition with his duty.
He that taketh not his cross — That is, whatever pain or inconvenience cannot be avoided, but by doing some evil, or omitting some good. Matt. xvi, 24; Luke xiv, 27.

He that findeth his life shall lose it — He that saves his life by denying me, shall lose it eternally; and he that loseth his life by confessing me, shall save it eternally. And as you shall be thus rewarded, so in proportion shall they who entertain you for my sake. Matt. xvi, 25; John xii, 25.

glossa.text: *The disciple is not,* etc. Do not disdain to bear what I bear, who am the Lord, doing what I will, and the master teaching what I know to be useful.

*If the master of the house.* He shows his own calumnies, that by his example they may bear injuries. Whence he said: *Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof. Beelzebub.* Beel is Bel himself, Zebub, a fly, etc., *as far as* the man of flies, or having flies.

*Therefore fear them not.* Their savagery or their blasphemies, because the day will come when God shall judge the hidden things of men, where both their wickedness shall be uncovered, and your intention, now known to God alone, shall be known by all.
*What I tell you.* That is, in what I wish you to be constant, etc., *as far as* the dwelling-place of the flesh being trodden underfoot, *preach ye.*

*Upon.* He speaks according to the custom of Palestine, etc., *as far as* tell it in the whole world. *Are not two sparrows?* Luke: *Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings ((Luc. XII))*? Nor is there much difference, seeing that two go for an as, and five for a dipondius. For a dipondius is out of two asses. And what one is in numbers, that the as is in weight: and what two is, that is the dipondius. *And one of them.* How then does the Apostle say: *Doth God take care for oxen ((Luc. IX))*? But care is one thing, knowledge another.
*Numbered.* That is, by the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* small and idle words should lie hidden from him.
*Whosoever shall confess.* Or a man confesses Jesus with that faith which works by love: he denies who does not obey the precepts of God.

*But he that.* He is denied by the Son before the Father, to whom there is not manifested, in the power of the divinity, the Son and the Father. He is confessed by the Son before the Father, who through the Son has access to the Father.
*Peace.* A good war was sent, that an evil peace might be broken.

*For I came.* Here Luke says: *There shall be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three shall be divided.* How then, etc., *as far as* circumcision and the other carnal observances. *To set apart.* That is, to extinguish the private affections of the flesh, by which men so love one another that they serve God the less. Or that they be utterly turned away, not that father and mother are not to be honoured, but after God; this is the order of charity.
*He that loveth father.* After God they are to be loved, but if both cannot be kept, hatred toward one's own is piety toward God.

*And he that taketh not,* etc. The cross is borne in two ways, etc., *as far as* the love of Christ may be shown. *And followeth me.* For one man mortifies the flesh for empty glory, or has a carnal compassion for his neighbour so as to favour his fault: he seems to bear the cross, but does not follow the Lord.
*He that findeth,* etc. By the name of the soul the present life is designated.

echoes.text: If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
echoes.note: To Cain: sin 'is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it.' Paul's 'do not let sin reign (basileueto) in your mortal body' (6:12) personifies Sin as a power seeking to master a person who must instead exercise dominion over it. The shared image of Sin as an external would-be ruler the believer must refuse to obey is striking; many read 6:12 against this primal scene.

echoes.text: Therefore tell the children of Israel, ‘I am Yahweh, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm, and with great judgments:
echoes.note: Redemption-from-bondage language: God brings Israel 'out from under the burdens' and 'redeems' them from slavery. Romans 6:6 ('no longer in bondage to sin', douleuein) and 6:7 ('freed from sin') run the exodus slavery/liberation pattern onto sin as the new Pharaoh. The slavery-redemption typology is strong thematically though the verbal contact here is diffuse; the fuller slavery exposition comes in 6:15-23.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: The valley of dry bones: God brings the dead up from their graves to new life by his Spirit. Paul's death-and-burial-then-'newness of life' (6:4) and 'alive from the dead' (6:13) share the figural movement of resurrection-as-new-existence, though Paul grounds it christologically rather than nationally.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh. I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and you shall keep my ordinances, and do them.
echoes.note: New heart and new spirit enabling obedience; 'newness of life' (6:4, kainotes zoes) coheres with the prophetic promise of interior renewal. Faint and disputed verbal contact, but the renewal/new-walk theme is shared.

echoes.text: After two days he will revive us. On the third day he will raise us up, and we will live before him.
echoes.note: 'After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.' A type of death-and-resurrection-to-life that early Christian reading connected to Christ's raising; resonates with 6:4-5,8-9 union in death and resurrection. Faint and contested.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Ahaziah fell down through the lattice in his upper room that was in Samaria, and was sick. So he sent messengers, and said to them, “Go, inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I will recover of this sickness.” But Yahweh’s angel said to Elijah the Tishbite, “Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria, and tell them, ‘Is it because there is no God in Israel, that you go to inquire of Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
echoes.note: 'Beelzebul' (10:25) derives from Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom Ahaziah consults. The name of the rejected foreign deity becomes the slander hurled at 'the master of the house'; the disciples should expect the same naming, 'how much more those of his household.'

echoes.text: “Don’t say, ‘A conspiracy!’ concerning all about which this people say, ‘A conspiracy!’ neither fear their threats, nor be terrorized. Yahweh of Armies is who you must respect as holy. He is the one you must fear. He is the one you must dread.
echoes.note: 'Neither fear ye their fear... Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear.' Isaiah's command to fear God rather than the conspiracy of men is the precise logic of 10:28: do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who can destroy soul and body. The double 'do not fear / rather fear' structure is Isaianic.

echoes.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire; which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind. Therefore behold, the days come”, says Yahweh, “that it shall no more be called Topheth, nor The valley of the son of Hinnom, but The valley of Slaughter; for they shall bury in Topheth, until there is no place to bury.
echoes.note: 'Gehenna' (10:28) is the valley of Hinnom (Topheth), the site of child-sacrifice that Jeremiah declares will become 'the valley of slaughter.' The OT condemnation of this valley as the place of fiery judgment supplies the term for the place where God can destroy both soul and body.

echoes.text: He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the children of Hinnom, that no man might make his son or his daughter to pass through the fire to Molech.
echoes.note: Josiah defiles Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom so none could pass a child through fire to Molech. Reinforces the Gehenna background as the defiled valley of fire that becomes the figure of final destruction (10:28).

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: 'There shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground.' The idiom of every hair guarded as a token of total providential protection (cf. 2 Sam 14:11; 1 Kgs 1:52) lies directly behind 10:30, 'the very hairs of your head are all numbered,' assuring the disciples of God's exhaustive care amid persecution.

echoes.text: You number my wanderings. You put my tears into your bottle. Aren’t they in your book?
echoes.note: God keeps count of the sufferer's wanderings and bottles his tears. A thematic analogue to the divine bookkeeping of hairs and the fall of sparrows (10:29-31) — God's minute attention to the afflicted — though without verbal overlap.

echoes.text: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
echoes.note: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' The wisdom maxim that proper fear is owed to God alone undergirds the redirection of fear in 10:28, but the connection is general rather than verbal.

echoes.text: I will also speak of your statutes before kings, and will not be disappointed.
echoes.note: 'I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.' A faint analogue to confessing Christ before men without shame (10:32), continuous with the 'testimony before governors and kings' of 10:18. Disputed and thematic only.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: 10:35-36 is a near-verbatim rendering of Micah 7:6: 'the son dishonoureth the father, the daughter riseth up against her mother, the daughter in law against her mother in law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.' Matthew reproduces the three paired antagonisms (father/son here as father, daughter/mother, daughter-in-law/mother-in-law) and the climactic 'a man's foes will be those of his own household' almost word for word. This is the strongest, formula-grade allusion in the chapter.

echoes.text: He said of his father, and of his mother, ‘I have not seen him.’ He didn’t acknowledge his brothers, nor did he know his own children; for they have observed your word, and keep your covenant.
echoes.note: Levi 'said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren... for they have observed thy word.' The blessing praises placing covenant loyalty above family bonds — the same demand as 10:37, loving God above father, mother, son, daughter. A recognized OT precedent for cult loyalty overriding kinship.

echoes.text: He said to them, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, ‘Every man put his sword on his thigh, and go back and forth from gate to gate throughout the camp, and every man kill his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbor.’” The sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. Moses said, “Consecrate yourselves today to Yahweh, yes, every man against his son, and against […]
echoes.note: The Levites slay brother, companion, and neighbor at Moses' command and are thereby 'consecrated.' A harsh background for loyalty to God dividing even kin (10:34-37); thematically apt but lexically distant and contested.

echoes.text: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!” He said, “Here I am.” He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.” Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and […]
echoes.note: The Aqedah — Abraham not withholding his son for the sake of God — is a possible figural backdrop to 'he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me' (10:37): supreme love of God above the dearest child. Suggestive typology rather than verbal echo.

lines: Hagar wept in the wilderness, her water gone.
And God heard the voice of the boy.
He opened her eyes, and there was a well.
The God who sees does not forget us.
Do not be afraid, says Jesus; even the sparrow is counted.
We are worth more than many sparrows.
Come, let us worship the God who hears.
We come, unafraid. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Picture the wilderness at noon — the skin of water empty, the throat dry, no shade and no road home.
The God who sees is here.
Hagar set the child under a bush and turned away, unable to watch him die — and God heard, and opened her eyes to a well.
The God who sees is here.
Jesus says the hairs of your head are numbered, and not one sparrow falls without your Father knowing.
The God who sees is here.
So whatever desert you crossed to get to this room, you were never out of God's sight for a moment.
The God who sees is here. Do not be afraid!

lines: Hagar's water was gone, the wilderness wide.
